title.value: Fluid Flow Simulation Tools for Complex Geological Models

note.value:
In this talk we will describe a set of tools developed to transform geological models into computational models for fluid flow simulations. The workflow has three main steps: geometrical representation of the geology, discretization of the flow equations, and the numerical solution of the associated nonlinear equations.

The first step is basically a mesh or grid generator. The objective here is to approximate the geology using simple geometrical elements (e.g., triangles, tetrahedrons, boxes, etc...). The majority of existing mesh generators are designed for the modeling of well-defined objects whose sizes do not span multiple length scales. Thus, many of the standard procedures are not suitable for use with complex geological structure such as faults and fractures. In the context of fluid flow modeling, it is however possible to introduce some geometrical simplification in the geology without significantly impacting the flow response. These simplifications are critical for the efficiency of the flow simulations. In this work we will present a gridding technique especially designed to model surfaces and their interactions. In our technique faults and fractures are represented using two-dimensional surfaces embedded in three-dimensional rock. In the second step, the equations describing fluid flow and transport in porous media are discretized on the grid representing the geology. We have developed a discretization technique based on a finite-volume formulation that uses an optimized two-point flux approximation for unstructured grids. In this technique faults and fractures are represented explicitly [1, 2]. Moreover, the resulting models can be simplified using specialized upscaling techniques [3, 4]. The third step concerns the solution of the corresponding nonlinear equations. In our methodology the result of the discretization is a list of connected pore-volumes. Connection “strengths” are quantified in terms of cell-to-cell transmissibilities, which are computed by our methods. The resulting flow model can be solved using any connectivity-based simulator. In this work we use Stanford’s General Purpose Research Simulator (GPRS) [5].

These techniques have been applied in several collaborative projects at Stanford between the Department of Energy Resources Engineering and the Geological and Environmental Sciences Department [6, 7, 8, 9]. Some of the results from these projects will be described in the talk.
Karimi-Fard, M. and Durlofsky, L.J. (2012). Fluid Flow Simulation Tools for Complex Geological Models. Stanford Digital Repository. Available at: http://purl.stanford.edu/yd952wx9756
